question: Define rape under Section 63 of the BNS. Explain the seven circumstances and the meaning of consent.
modelAnswer: Under Section 63, a man commits rape if he does any of four kinds of act to a woman: (a) penetration of his penis, to any extent, into her vagina, mouth, urethra or anus, or makes her do so with him or another; (b) insertion of any object or body part other than the penis into her vagina, urethra or anus; (c) manipulation of any part of her body to cause penetration; or (d) application of his mouth to her vagina, anus or urethra. The act must be done in one of seven circumstances: (i) against her will; (ii) without her consent; (iii) with consent obtained by putting her or someone she cares about in fear of death or hurt; (iv) with consent given because she believes he is the man she is, or believes she is, lawfully married to; (v) with consent given when, because of unsoundness of mind, intoxication or a stupefying substance, she cannot understand its nature and consequences; (vi) with or without her consent when she is under eighteen; and (vii) when she is unable to communicate consent. Explanation 2 defines consent as an unequivocal voluntary agreement communicated by words, gestures or any verbal or non-verbal means, and the proviso makes clear that a woman who does not physically resist is not, for that reason alone, taken to consent. Explanation 1 says 'vagina' includes the labia majora. There are two Exceptions: a medical procedure or intervention is not rape, and sexual acts by a man with his own wife are not rape unless she is under eighteen.

question: Discuss the scheme of punishment for rape under Sections 64, 65, 66, 70 and 71 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: The BNS grades punishment for rape by the offender's position, the victim's age and the harm caused. Section 64(1) prescribes rigorous imprisonment of at least ten years, which may extend to life, and fine. Section 64(2) covers aggravated cases — rape by a police officer within his station limits or on a woman in custody, by a public servant on a woman in custody, by armed forces in an area of deployment, by jail, remand home, institution or hospital staff, by a relative, guardian, teacher or person in trust or authority, during communal or sectarian violence, on a pregnant woman, on a woman incapable of consent or with a disability, by a person in control or dominance, rape causing grievous bodily harm, and repeated rape. The minimum remains ten years but the maximum is life imprisonment for the remainder of natural life. Section 65 raises the minimum to twenty years where the victim is under sixteen, and allows death where she is under twelve; the fine must meet medical and rehabilitation expenses and is paid to the victim. Section 66 applies when rape under s.64 causes death or a persistent vegetative state: twenty years to life for natural life, or death. Section 70 deems each member of a group to have committed rape (minimum twenty years), and where the woman is under eighteen prescribes life for natural life or death. Finally, s.71 punishes a person convicted again under ss.64, 65, 66 or 70 with life for the remainder of natural life, or death. All these offences are cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session.

question: What is new in Section 69 of the BNS? Distinguish it from rape under Section 63.
modelAnswer: Section 69 has no equivalent in the IPC. It punishes a person who has sexual intercourse with a woman by deceitful means, or by promising to marry her without any intention of keeping the promise, where the intercourse does not amount to rape. The Explanation says deceitful means include inducement for, or a false promise of, employment or promotion, and marrying by suppressing identity. The punishment is imprisonment up to ten years and fine; it is cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session. The difference from rape lies in the nature of the woman's agreement. Rape under s.63 involves an act against her will, without consent, or with consent vitiated in one of the ways listed (fear, impersonation of a husband, incapacity, age under eighteen). Section 69 covers cases where she agrees, but her agreement was obtained through deceit about marriage, a job or identity. Section 69 applies only where the act does not already amount to rape.

question: Explain the offences of sexual harassment, voyeurism and stalking under Sections 75, 77 and 78.
modelAnswer: Sexual harassment (s.75) is committed by a man who (i) makes physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures, (ii) demands or requests sexual favours, (iii) shows pornography to a woman against her will, or (iv) makes sexually coloured remarks. The first three are punishable with rigorous imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both; the fourth with imprisonment up to one year, or fine, or both. Voyeurism (s.77) is watching or capturing an image of a woman engaged in a private act in circumstances where she would expect not to be observed, or disseminating such an image. A 'private act' includes a situation where her genitals, posterior or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear, where she is using a lavatory, or where she is doing a sexual act not ordinarily done in public. Explanation 2 provides that consent to the image being captured is not consent to its being shared. The punishment is one to three years and fine on first conviction, and three to seven years on a subsequent conviction. Stalking (s.78) is committed by a man who follows a woman and repeatedly contacts or tries to contact her despite a clear indication of disinterest, or who monitors her use of the internet, e-mail or electronic communication. The accused may escape liability by proving that the conduct was for preventing or detecting crime under State authority, was done under a law, or was reasonable and justified. Punishment is up to three years and fine on first conviction (bailable) and up to five years on a subsequent conviction (non-bailable).

question: What is 'dowry death' under Section 80? State its ingredients and punishment.
modelAnswer: Section 80(1) defines dowry death. Its ingredients are: (1) the death of a woman caused by burns or bodily injury, or occurring otherwise than under normal circumstances; (2) within seven years of her marriage; (3) it is shown that soon before her death she was subjected to cruelty or harassment; (4) by her husband or any relative of her husband; (5) for, or in connection with, any demand for dowry. When these are shown, the death is called a 'dowry death' and the husband or relative is deemed to have caused it. 'Dowry' has the meaning given in s.2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. Under s.80(2) the punishment is imprisonment of at least seven years, which may extend to imprisonment for life. The offence is cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session. The provision corresponds to s.304B IPC. It is often charged together with cruelty under s.85, which does not require death.

question: Explain cruelty by a husband or his relatives under Sections 85 and 86. How is the offence classified?
modelAnswer: Section 85 punishes a husband, or a relative of the husband, who subjects a woman to cruelty, with imprisonment up to three years and fine. Section 86 defines cruelty for this purpose in two limbs: (a) any wilful conduct of a nature likely to drive the woman to suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to her life, limb or health, mental or physical; or (b) harassment of the woman aimed at coercing her or any relative of hers to meet an unlawful demand for property or valuable security, or on account of a failure to meet such a demand. Under the BNSS First Schedule, the offence is cognizable if information is given to the officer in charge of a police station by the aggrieved woman, or by a person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption, or, if there is no such relative, by a public servant of a notified class. It is non-bailable, not compoundable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. These sections correspond to s.498A IPC and its Explanation.

question: Discuss bigamy under Section 82 of the BNS, including its Exception.
modelAnswer: Under s.82(1), whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in a case where that marriage is void because it takes place during the life of the existing spouse, is punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine. The ingredients are an earlier valid marriage, the spouse being alive, a second marriage, and the second marriage being void for that reason. The Exception excludes two situations: where the earlier marriage has been declared void by a court of competent jurisdiction, and where the earlier spouse has been continually absent for seven years and not heard of as alive within that time — but only if the person marrying again informs the new partner of the real facts before the marriage. Section 82(2) raises the punishment to up to ten years and fine where the former marriage is concealed from the new partner. Both are non-cognizable, bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. The offence under s.82(1) may be compounded, with the court's permission, by the husband or wife of the person who married again. The section combines ss.494 and 495 IPC.

question: Explain the offences relating to causing miscarriage under Sections 88 to 92.
modelAnswer: Section 88 punishes whoever voluntarily causes a woman with child to miscarry, unless done in good faith to save her life: up to three years, or fine, or both, and up to seven years and fine if she is quick with child. The Explanation makes a woman who causes her own miscarriage liable. It is non-cognizable, bailable and compoundable by the woman with the court's permission. Section 89 applies where the miscarriage is caused without the woman's consent, whether or not she is quick with child: life imprisonment, or up to ten years and fine. Section 90(1) punishes an act done with intent to cause miscarriage which causes the woman's death with up to ten years and fine; under s.90(2), if done without her consent, life imprisonment or that punishment. Knowledge that the act was likely to cause death is not needed. Section 91 punishes an act before birth intended to prevent a child from being born alive or to cause it to die after birth, and which has that result, unless done in good faith to save the mother's life: up to ten years, or fine, or both. Section 92 punishes an act that would amount to culpable homicide if it caused death and which causes the death of a quick unborn child: up to ten years and fine. Terminations lawfully carried out under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 fall outside these offences.

question: What offences against children are dealt with in Sections 93 to 99? Which of them is new?
modelAnswer: Section 93 punishes a parent or person having care of a child under twelve who exposes or leaves the child anywhere intending to abandon it wholly: up to seven years, or fine, or both; a trial for murder or culpable homicide remains possible if the child dies. Section 94 punishes secretly burying or disposing of a child's dead body to conceal its birth: up to two years, or fine, or both. Section 95 is new: hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence is punishable with three to ten years and fine, and if the offence is committed the person is also punished as if he had committed it himself; using a child for sexual exploitation or pornography is covered. Section 96 punishes inducing a child to go anywhere or do any act intending or knowing that it will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse: up to ten years and fine. Section 97 punishes kidnapping or abducting a child under ten to dishonestly take movable property from its person: up to seven years and fine. Sections 98 and 99 punish selling or buying a child for prostitution, illicit intercourse or any unlawful and immoral purpose — up to ten years for selling, and seven to fourteen years for buying — with presumptions of intent where a girl under eighteen is disposed of to, or obtained by, a prostitute or brothel-keeper.

question: How does the BNS protect the identity of victims of sexual offences? Explain Sections 72 and 73.
modelAnswer: Section 72(1) makes it an offence to print or publish the name, or anything that may reveal the identity, of a person against whom an offence under ss.64 to 71 is alleged or found to have been committed, punishable with up to two years and fine. Section 72(2) permits disclosure only (a) by or under a written order of the officer in charge of the police station or the investigating officer, acting in good faith for the investigation; (b) by, or with the written authorisation of, the victim; or (c) where the victim is dead, a child or of unsound mind, by or with the written authorisation of the next of kin — who may give it only to the chairman or secretary of a welfare institution or organisation recognised by the Central or State Government. Section 73 separately punishes printing or publishing any matter relating to court proceedings concerning such an offence without the court's previous permission, also with up to two years and fine; publishing the judgment of a High Court or the Supreme Court is not an offence. Both are cognizable, bailable and triable by any Magistrate. They correspond to s.228A IPC.
